title: NestJS Authentication Guards
readme:
FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE
Volume 05 - Authentication & Security
Phase 18 - NestJS Authentication Guards

This phase closes the trust gap between the authenticated Next.js application and the separate NestJS API.

Primary implementation: @supabase/supabase-js 2.116.0 auth.getClaims(jwt) + custom NestJS 12 guard.

Important: access tokens and secret keys in examples are placeholders only. Never commit real credentials.

lessons.body:
From Session to Trusted API
Identity
Why a Next.js login is not enough for NestJS

Phase 18 trust boundary

Next.js authenticated session

Authorization: Bearer <access token>

NestJS authentication guard

Verified Supabase identity

Controller and business service

Course principle: a user ID becomes trusted only after the access token has been cryptographically
verified by the backend.

Two separate trust boundaries
TaskFlow has two server processes. Next.js can read its cookie-backed Supabase session, while
NestJS receives an ordinary HTTP request. NestJS must establish trust independently.

Different servers, different responsibilities

Next.js                                                      NestJS

• cookie session                                            • receives headers

• refresh lifecycle                                         • no cookie knowledge assumed

• Supabase SSR client                                       • must verify bearer JWT

• can obtain access token                                   • creates request identity

Wrong architecture
GET /tasks?userId=5c53...

// Browser claims who the user is.
// The API trusts an unverified identifier.

A UUID is not proof of identity. Anyone can send someone else's UUID.

Correct architecture
Identity establishment

Next.js gets current access token

Authorization: Bearer <JWT>

NestJS extracts bearer token

Supabase verification validates JWT

Verified sub becomes authenticated user id

Authentication vs authorization
Question                             Layer                              Typical result

Who is calling?                      Auth guard                         401 when not authenticated

May this user access this resource?
Authorization/business layer            403 when authenticated but forbidden

Is the requested workflow valid?Service/business rules                  400/409 depending on rule

The trust statement

After verification, claims.sub may be used as the authenticated Supabase user identifier. Before
verification, decoded JWT contents are attacker-controlled input.

Source note: verified against current Supabase Auth/getClaims/signing-key guidance and NestJS
authentication/authorization docs. Full URLs and version notes are included in SOURCE_NOTES.txt.

lessons.title: Server Side Supabase Token Verification
lessons.summary: PHASE 18 - BOOK 03 Server-Side Supabase Token Verification Using getClaims() in a NestJS 12-compatible service Phase 18 trust boundary Next.js authenticated session Authorization: Bearer <access token> NestJS authentication guard Verified Supabase identity Controller and business service Course principle: a user ID becomes trusted only…
lessons.body:
Server-Side Supabase Token
Verification
Using getClaims() in a NestJS 12-compatible service

Phase 18 trust boundary

Next.js authenticated session

Authorization: Bearer <access token>

NestJS authentication guard

Verified Supabase identity

Controller and business service

Course principle: a user ID becomes trusted only after the access token has been cryptographically
verified by the backend.

Why getClaims()
Supabase documents auth.getClaims(jwt) as the preferred way to verify Supabase-issued JWTs. With
asymmetric signing keys it verifies against the project JWKS and benefits from caching; with legacy
symmetric signing it can fall back to the Auth server.

Install in apps/api
cd "C:\path\to\taskflow\apps\api"

pnpm add @supabase/supabase-js@2.116.0

Environment
# apps/api/.env
SUPABASE_URL=https://<project-ref>.supabase.co
SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=sb_publishable_...

The publishable key is not a privileged server secret. It identifies the project/client context; the user JWT
proves the caller identity. Do not use a Supabase secret/service-role key merely to verify ordinary user

access tokens.

Verification service
// auth/supabase-auth.service.ts
import { Injectable, UnauthorizedException } from '@nestjs/common'
import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config'
import { createClient } from '@supabase/supabase-js'

@Injectable()
export class SupabaseAuthService {
private readonly url: string
private readonly client

constructor(config: ConfigService) {
this.url = config.getOrThrow<string>('SUPABASE_URL')
const key = config.getOrThrow<string>(
'SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY',
)

this.client = createClient(this.url, key, {
auth: {
persistSession: false,
autoRefreshToken: false,
},
})
}

async verifyAccessToken(token: string) {
const { data, error } =
await this.client.auth.getClaims(token)

if (error || !data?.claims?.sub) {
throw new UnauthorizedException(
'Invalid or expired access token',
)
}

const expectedIssuer = `${this.url}/auth/v1`
if (data.claims.iss !== expectedIssuer) {
throw new UnauthorizedException('Invalid token issuer')
}

return data.claims
}
}

Why extra issuer checking?
getClaims() performs cryptographic verification. We still keep the expected project issuer explicit in
TaskFlow so a token from another Supabase project cannot silently become an application identity.

Audience / role policy
For ordinary TaskFlow users, require a user access token whose audience/role corresponds to the
authenticated user context. The exact claims are read from the verified payload, never from an
unverified decode.
Source note: verified against current Supabase Auth/getClaims/signing-key guidance and NestJS
authentication/authorization docs. Full URLs and version notes are included in SOURCE_NOTES.txt.

lessons.summary: PHASE 18 - BOOK 07 401 Error Semantics Making authentication failures predictable and safe Phase 18 trust boundary Next.js authenticated session Authorization: Bearer <access token> NestJS authentication guard Verified Supabase identity Controller and business service Course principle: a user ID becomes trusted only after the…
lessons.body:
401 Error Semantics
Making authentication failures predictable and safe

Phase 18 trust boundary

Next.js authenticated session

Authorization: Bearer <access token>

NestJS authentication guard

Verified Supabase identity

Controller and business service

Course principle: a user ID becomes trusted only after the access token has been cryptographically
verified by the backend.

Authentication failure matrix
Scenario                                 HTTP     Public meaning

No Authorization header                  401      Authentication required

Wrong auth scheme                        401      Bearer token required

Expired token                            401      Authentication expired

Invalid signature                        401      Credentials invalid

Wrong issuer/project                     401      Credentials invalid

Verified user lacks permission           403      Authenticated but forbidden

Do not leak verification internals
A client does not need to know whether signature verification failed because of a key ID, algorithm, or
JWK cache detail. Keep precise diagnostics in safe server logs and return a stable public 401 contract.

Phase 13 integration

The guard can throw UnauthorizedException. The existing global exception filter then adds TaskFlow
fields such as requestId, timestamp, path, and stable error code.
{
"statusCode": 401,
"code": "UNAUTHORIZED",
"message": "Authentication required.",
"requestId": "42",
"path": "/tasks",
"timestamp": "2026-09-18T..."
}

Frontend behavior
• 401: refresh/re-establish session or redirect to login.

• 403: show an authorization/permission message; logging in again may not help.

• Network failure: do not mislabel it as authentication failure.

401 and 403 must remain distinct. Authentication and authorization are different security decisions.

authentication/authorization docs. Full URLs and version notes are included in SOURCE_NOTES.txt.

lessons.title: CORS Authorization Headers and Preflight
lessons.summary: PHASE 18 - BOOK 08 CORS and Authorization Headers Why browser bearer requests can trigger preflight Phase 18 trust boundary Next.js authenticated session Authorization: Bearer <access token> NestJS authentication guard Verified Supabase identity Controller and business service Course principle: a user ID becomes trusted only…
lessons.body:
CORS and Authorization Headers
Why browser bearer requests can trigger preflight

Phase 18 trust boundary

Next.js authenticated session

Authorization: Bearer <access token>

NestJS authentication guard

Verified Supabase identity

Controller and business service

Course principle: a user ID becomes trusted only after the access token has been cryptographically
verified by the backend.

Browser path

Cross-origin authenticated request

Browser Client Component

OPTIONS preflight when required

NestJS CORS policy

Actual request with Authorization

AuthGuard verifies token

NestJS CORS configuration
app.enableCors({
origin: 'http://localhost:3000',
methods: ['GET', 'POST', 'PATCH', 'DELETE', 'OPTIONS'],
allowedHeaders: [
'Content-Type',
'Authorization',
],
})

Important distinction
CORS does not verify the access token. CORS controls whether browser JavaScript may make/read
cross-origin requests. The AuthGuard verifies authentication.

Server-to-server path
A Next.js Server Component calling NestJS from the server is not subject to the browser's CORS
enforcement. The bearer token still must be verified because CORS and authentication solve different
problems.

Common debugging sequence
• Does Network show an OPTIONS request?

• Does the preflight response allow Authorization?

• Does the actual request contain Authorization: Bearer ...?

• Does NestJS return 401 from the guard or was the browser blocked before the request?

authentication/authorization docs. Full URLs and version notes are included in SOURCE_NOTES.txt.

Signing Keys, JWKS, Rotation and
2026 Supabase Choices
Understanding what getClaims() is doing for you

Phase 18 trust boundary

Next.js authenticated session

Authorization: Bearer <access token>

NestJS authentication guard

Verified Supabase identity

Controller and business service

Course principle: a user ID becomes trusted only after the access token has been cryptographically
verified by the backend.

Modern Supabase signing keys
Supabase now supports asymmetric signing keys and publishes trusted public keys through the
project JWKS endpoint. Public keys verify tokens but cannot mint new ones.
GET https://<project-ref>.supabase.co/
auth/v1/.well-known/jwks.json

Why getClaims() fits this course
Concern                               getClaims() behavior

Asymmetric keys                       Verifies against JWKS, with caching

Key rotation                          Supabase client handles JWK lookup/cache behavior

Legacy HS256                          Falls back to Auth server verification

NestJS version                        Framework-independent base client call

Alternative: direct jose verification
For projects committed to asymmetric signing keys, a backend can use a JWT library such as jose with
a remote JWKS and explicitly validate issuer, audience and expiration. Supabase documents this
pattern. We do not choose it as the primary course implementation because getClaims() also handles
legacy signing-key projects.

@supabase/server in 2026
Supabase now recommends @supabase/server for bearer-token backend APIs and ships a NestJS adapter.
Version 1.x is public beta. At the time of this phase, the package adapter table lists NestJS 10 and 11,
while TaskFlow is NestJS 12. We therefore use the framework-independent verification path and can revisit
the adapter after its published compatibility catches up.

Revocation nuance
JWKS caching improves performance but means emergency signing-key revocation can have a cache
window in external backend verifiers. Supabase documents this trade-off; incident-response plans
should account for it.

Implement, verify, explain, then prepare for authorization

Phase 18 trust boundary

Next.js authenticated session

Authorization: Bearer <access token>

NestJS authentication guard

Controller and business service

Level 1 - Follow
Install the backend Supabase client, add API environment variables, create SupabaseAuthService,
create the guard, add @CurrentUser(), and protect /auth/me.

Level 2 - Modify
Protect TasksController at controller level. Keep /health public. Verify the no-token and valid-token
paths.

Level 3 - Implement
Build an authenticated GET /auth/me response that returns only safe verified identity fields. Add a
frontend page that calls it from Next.js using the current access token.

Level 4 - Engineer
Design the production authentication policy for a payroll API containing public health checks,
employee endpoints, HR endpoints, and internal automation endpoints. Decide whether auth should

be global/default-deny and identify which endpoints truly need different credential types.

Phase exit oral questions
• Why is a userId query parameter not identity?

• What exactly turns claims.sub into trusted identity?

• Why is decode-only JWT handling unsafe?

• Why does a 401 differ from a 403?

• Why is CORS not authentication?

• Why do we keep authorization out of AuthGuard?

• When would direct JWKS verification be appropriate?

Exit checklist
• Valid Supabase token reaches NestJS as a Bearer token.

• Missing/malformed/expired tokens return 401.

• Verified sub is attached as request user.id.

• Protected Tasks routes reject anonymous callers.

• Health route remains public.

• No access token or secret key is committed/logged.

• You can explain the difference between authentication, authorization and business rules.

Phase 18 is complete when NestJS can establish a trusted caller identity independently of the browser and
independently of Next.js.

Guided Build Lab — Phase 18: NestJS Authentication Guards

lessons.title: Debugging Workshop
lessons.summary:
Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.
lessons.body:
Debugging Workshop — Phase 18: NestJS Authentication Guards

Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.

The debugging loop
1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action.
2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state.
3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior.
4. Form one hypothesis.
5. Change one variable.
6. Re-run the same reproduction.
7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis.

Boundary walk
Next.js session -> Bearer access token -> NestJS guard -> Supabase/JWT verification -> trusted request user -> controller/service

Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next.

Failure drill 1 — Trusting userId from request body/query
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 2 — Decoding JWT without signature verification
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 3 — Returning 403 when no valid authentication exists
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 4 — Logging bearer tokens during debugging
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Do not hide the evidence
Avoid immediately clearing caches, deleting lockfiles, resetting the database, disabling security checks, or reinstalling everything. Those actions may erase the evidence that teaches you what was wrong. Use them only after you can explain why they are relevant.

lessons.title: Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge
lessons.summary:
Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 18 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?
lessons.body:
Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — NestJS Authentication Guards

Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 18 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?

Required outcome
Make NestJS independently verify Supabase access tokens and attach trusted identity before protected handlers run.

Required artifact
Authentication guard + verification service + current-user helper + protected /auth/me and task routes.

Constraints
• Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch.
• Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt.
• Keep changes scoped to the capability.
• Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases.
• Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable.

Acceptance criteria
• Can explain why Next.js login is not enough for the API.
• Can trace guard execution.
• Can distinguish 401 and 403.
• Can prove identity is derived from verified token claims.

Independent build sequence
1. Add Authorization: Bearer token handling in the API client without putting tokens in URLs/logs.
2. Extract and validate the bearer scheme in a guard with clear missing/malformed behavior.
3. Verify the token server-side using the supported Supabase/JWT verification path.
4. Normalize verified claims into an application user identity object.
5. Attach identity once and expose it through a typed decorator/helper rather than reparsing tokens in services.
6. Protect /auth/me and one task endpoint; test valid, missing, malformed, expired, and wrong-project tokens.

Self-review
Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence.

Stretch challenge
Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly.

Phase exit
Run the relevant checks, inspect Git diff, and write a three-sentence summary: what the system can do now, which boundary owns the new responsibility, and which failure you now know how to diagnose. Only then mark the phase complete.

lessons.title: Mastery Capstone Lab
lessons.summary: Integrate Phase 18 without following a transcript.
lessons.body:
Mastery Capstone Lab

This is the transfer exercise for Phase 18: NestJS Authentication Guards. The detailed lessons are now closed-book reference material. Your task is to prove that the phase outcome can be reproduced from requirements, repository evidence, and debugging—not by copying a finished implementation.

Target artifact
Authentication guard + verification service + current-user helper + protected /auth/me and task routes.

Acceptance criteria
- Write the behavior and constraints before implementation.
- Identify the owning layer and every boundary crossed.
- Implement the smallest complete vertical slice.
- Verify the happy path from outside the implementation.
- Demonstrate at least one expected failure path.
- Run the phase-relevant quality checks.
- Review the diff for accidental duplication, leaked responsibilities, missing validation/authorization, and hidden environment assumptions.

Evidence packet
Save the command/request used, expected result, actual result, one failure reproduction, the fix, and a short explanation of why the final responsibility belongs where it does. This packet is more valuable than a screenshot of a green page because it demonstrates repeatable engineering reasoning.

Stretch
Change one requirement after the first implementation. Measure which files must change. If a tiny domain change causes unrelated layers to move, use that evidence to discuss coupling before adding another abstraction.
